title: Gold
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/0/body: **XAU/USD** is the price of **one troy ounce** of gold in US dollars. XAU is gold's international code (AU comes from the Latin word Aurum). A price of 2,400 means one ounce of gold costs $2,400.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/0/tip: A troy ounce (about 31.1 grams) is different from a regular ounce (about 28.3 grams).
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/1/body: Gold pays no interest or dividends. The **real interest rate** is the nominal rate minus inflation. When it **rises**, holding gold instead of high-yield bonds has a bigger "opportunity cost", and gold usually comes **under pressure**.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/1/tip: Falling real rates usually help gold. But that's a tendency, not a rule.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/2/prompt: The nominal bond yield is 4% and expected inflation is 4.5%. What's the real interest rate, and what does it mean for gold?
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/2/options/0: -0.5%; usually a friendlier backdrop for gold
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/2/options/3: +8.5%; usually a friendly backdrop for gold
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/2/explanation: 4% − 4.5% = −0.5%. When the real rate is negative, bonds don't really protect your buying power, and the opportunity cost of holding gold drops.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/3/statement: Since gold pays no interest, rising real interest rates are usually bad for gold.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/3/explanation: When bonds pay a higher real yield, some investors put aside gold, which pays nothing. That's why gold usually comes under pressure.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/4/title: The dollar, fear and central banks
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/4/body: Gold is priced in **dollars**, so a stronger dollar usually puts **pressure** on gold. In times of **fear and crisis**, demand for gold usually rises. **Central banks** have also been big gold buyers in recent years, supporting demand.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/4/tip: These are tendencies. In a severe crisis, for example, the dollar and gold sometimes rise together.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/5/pairs/0/meani: Bigger opportunity cost of holding gold
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/5/pairs/1/meani: Gold gets cheaper for the rest of the world
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/6/prompt: The highlighted candle formed right after a big US news release. Which news fits this gold move?
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/6/explanation: Hot inflation raises expectations of higher rates. Bond yields and the dollar rise, and gold usually drops. The other three options usually help gold.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/7/prompt: The Fed made a surprise rate cut, bond yields fell and the dollar weakened. What's the more likely reaction in gold?
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/7/options/0: Usually leans up; both factors help gold
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/7/options/1: Usually leans down; a weak dollar hurts gold
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/7/options/2: Usually leans down; lower rates mean less demand
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/7/options/3: No effect; gold only reacts to war news
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/7/explanation: Lower rates cut the opportunity cost of holding gold, and a weak dollar makes gold cheaper for the rest of the world. Two factors pointing the same way make a rise more likely, but not certain.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/8/statement: The gold–dollar relationship is a hard rule: the two never rise at the same time.
lessons/gold-u1-l1/steps/8/explanation: The inverse link between gold and the dollar is only a tendency. In some crises, both attract buyers at the same time as safe assets.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/title: Size and move value in gold
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/0/title: How big is a gold lot?
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/0/body: At most brokers, **1 standard lot** of XAU/USD equals **100 ounces** of gold. So every **$1** price move makes **$100** profit or loss per lot.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/0/tip: Check the contract specification at your own broker. Not all brokers are the same.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/1/prompt: You bought 0.5 lot of gold at $2,400 and closed at $2,412. How much did you make?
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/1/explanation: Price rose $12 and you hold 50 ounces: 12 × 50 = $600.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/2/body: Gold usually has a bigger **daily range** than EUR/USD, both in percent and in dollars per lot. So with the **same size**, a gold trade can carry several times the risk.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/2/example/resul: Trade gold with a smaller size
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/2/tip: In gold, count in dollars instead of "pips". The definition of a gold pip isn't the same across brokers.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/3/prompt: You entered 0.2 lot of gold at the lines on the chart. If your stop loss is hit, how much do you lose?
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/3/explanation: Entry to stop loss is $10, and 0.2 lot is 20 ounces: 10 × 20 = $200. ($400 is the target profit: 20 × 20, a 1:2 ratio.)
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/4/title: Size your trade from your risk
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/4/body: **Size (lots) = risk amount ÷ (stop loss distance in dollars × 100)**. Say you want to risk $100 and your stop loss is $5 from your entry: 100 ÷ (5 × 100) = **0.2 lot**.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/4/tip: The 100 is the size of one lot at most brokers. If yours is different, use its number.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/5/prompt: Your account is $5,000 and you want to risk 1%. Your stop loss on gold is $10 from your entry. What's the right size?
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/5/explanation: Your allowed risk is $50, and 1 lot loses 10 × 100 = $1,000 at the stop: 50 ÷ 1,000 = 0.05 lot (5 ounces).
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/6/statement: If you trade 1 lot on EUR/USD, 1 lot of gold carries about the same risk.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/6/explanation: A normal daily gold move with 1 lot can be several thousand dollars, while a similar EUR/USD move is a few hundred. Always size from your risk and stop loss distance.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/7/sentence: At most brokers 1 lot of gold is ___ ounces, so with 0.1 lot each $1 move is worth $___ in profit or loss.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/7/explanation: 1 lot = 100 ounces and 0.1 lot = 10 ounces, so each $1 move × 10 ounces = $10.
lessons/gold-u1-l2/steps/8/prompt: Gold went from $2,400 to $2,460 in a week. By what percent did it rise?
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/0/body: When **fear** rises (war, banking crises, stock crashes), money usually flows into **safe-haven assets**: gold, the Japanese yen, the Swiss franc and US government bonds. This mood is called **risk-off**.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/1/prompt: Sudden news of military tension just broke. Tap the candle where gold reacted to the news.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/1/explanation: The market was calm before, with small candles. Then a huge bullish candle suddenly appeared. That's the moment safe-haven demand poured into gold.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/2/body: A news spike in gold sometimes keeps going, and sometimes quickly **reverses** once the fear fades. During news the **spread** also widens and you may get **slippage**, meaning your order fills at a worse price.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/2/tip: Chasing a news candle without a stop loss is one of the most expensive mistakes.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/3/prompt: Which group is made up entirely of traditional safe-haven assets?
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/3/options/3: Japanese yen, New Zealand dollar, copper
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/3/explanation: Gold, the yen and the franc usually attract buyers in risk-off. The Australian and New Zealand dollars, oil, copper and tech stocks are more risk-sensitive assets.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/4/statement: A gold spike after scary news always keeps going, so buying at the top of the news candle is low risk.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/4/explanation: Many news spikes pull back once the fear fades. Buying at the top of a big candle means a distant stop loss and high risk.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/5/pairs/2/meani: An asset whose demand rises in a crisis
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/5/pairs/3/meani: An order filled at a worse price than expected
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/6/prompt: US real bond yields have been falling for weeks and global tensions are high. After an uptrend, gold is back at support, and the last candle is a hammer. What do you do?
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/6/explanation: Two fundamental factors (falling real yields and safe-haven demand) line up with the technical picture (uptrend, pullback to support and a hammer), so a continued rise is more likely. It's still not certain, and you need a stop loss below the hammer's low.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/7/prompt: Put the steps for preparing to trade gold in a news-heavy week in order.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/7/items/0: Check the economic calendar and key news
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/7/items/1: Write down your bullish and bearish scenarios in advance
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/7/items/2: Set your stop loss in dollars
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/7/items/3: Work out your size from your risk amount
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/7/items/4: After entry, manage the trade by your plan
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/7/explanation: First you need to know what news is coming, then build scenarios. Size always comes after the stop loss is set, because it depends on it.
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/8/prompt: At midnight, news breaks of an unexpected military clash: stock indexes drop, the yen strengthens and US bond yields fall. What's the most sensible read for gold?
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/8/options/0: Safe-haven demand and falling yields both usually help gold
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/8/options/1: Falling stocks mean gold will probably fall too
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/8/options/2: Falling bond yields usually hurt gold
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/8/options/3: Gold only reacts to central bank decisions
lessons/gold-u1-l3/steps/8/explanation: Risk-off lifts safe-haven demand, and falling yields cut the opportunity cost of holding gold. Still, the reaction can be temporary, so you still need risk management.
